Visual walkthrough: one Birmingham catchment, four stages

Source: vignettes/visual-walkthrough.qmd 
library(catchmentACS)
library(sf)

fixture <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "visual_walkthrough_fixture.rds",
                                package = "catchmentACS"))
ANCHOR <- fixture$anchor_site
ANCHOR
[1] "AL_BHM_01"

Why a visual walkthrough

cacs_run() hands you a tidy table: one row per site per rate, with an estimate and a margin of error. That table tells you what a site’s neighborhood looks like, but it hides how the package got there — the drive-time polygon it drew, the Census tracts it clipped, and the weights it used to blend them. When a reviewer or co-author asks “how exactly did you turn one address into a poverty rate?”, a table is a hard thing to point at.

This article answers that question with maps. It opens up that one line of code and follows a single, real site — the Vulcan statue in Birmingham, Alabama (site AL_BHM_01, Birmingham_Vulcan, on Red Mountain just south of downtown, the same site exercised in the package’s verified v0.3.0 workflow run) — through the four spatial stages that turn one point on a map into neighborhood statistics:

  1. Isochrone — draw the area a family can reach from the site in ten minutes of driving.
  2. Intersection — find every Census tract that area touches, and how much of each one falls inside it.
  3. Weighted variable — pool one ACS variable across those tracts, weighting each tract by its overlap.
  4. Rates — collapse the whole catchment into five headline rates, each with a margin of error.

Each stage is drawn as one interactive leaflet map, so you can watch the computation happen for a place you can picture. Where vignette("getting-started", package = "catchmentACS") shows the ergonomics of the one-line call, this article traces the geometry inside it. Every map is paired with a short “what to look for” note that names the exact spatial feature to read off the picture. We stay at the map level here; the math behind area weighting and MOE propagation lives in ?cacs_propagate_moe and vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS").

The maps are a frozen real-data snapshot

Every map below is built from one small bundled file, visual_walkthrough_fixture.rds, so this article renders fully offline — no Census, OSRM, ORS, or other network call is made. The snapshot holds real data: a real ten-minute OSRM drive-time isochrone around the Vulcan, plus the real surrounding Birmingham-area Census tracts and American Community Survey (ACS) estimates it overlaps, captured once and frozen so the figures reproduce exactly. It is one recognizable catchment, not a synthetic toy — but it is also a single moment in time, a teaching snapshot rather than a live policy estimate. A real analysis of your own sites needs a fresh live run against a routing provider and the Census API (see vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS")). To reuse these maps on your own data, hand a cacs_run() result and its inputs to the same five plotting functions in place of fixture.

Stage 1 — the isochrone

The first stage answers the most basic question: what, spatially, is this site’s catchment? An isochrone is the drive-time catchment polygon: the area you can reach from the site within a set number of minutes. For the Vulcan we use a single ten-minute drive-time ring, so the map reads as one connected reachable area rather than a set of nested bands. The red marker is the site; click it to read its site_id, name, and coordinates. The shaded polygon is everywhere a car can get to in ten minutes on the road network. (In a live run, OSRM is the default routing provider, ORS is available with an API key, and Mapbox and r5r are reserved fail-loud names — see vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS").)

cacs_plot_site_isochrone(
  site_id  = ANCHOR,
  iso_sf   = fixture$iso_sf,
  sites_df = fixture$sites_df
)

What to look for. Read the shape and reach of the ten-minute polygon. Notice that it is not a tidy circle: it stretches along the interstates and arterials that radiate from Red Mountain and pinches in where the terrain or the street grid slows a driver down. That asymmetry is the whole point of a drive-time catchment — it follows the road network, not a compass, so it captures who can actually get to the site rather than who happens to live within a fixed radius. The polygon’s footprint is the geographic area this site is, in effect, responsible for, and it is what the next three stages fill in with population data.

Stage 2 — intersection and area weight

Stage 2 answers how much of each Census tract falls inside the catchment? The ten-minute polygon is overlaid on every tract it touches and intersected with them in an equal-area projection (EPSG:5070). Each tract is then shaded by its area weight,

\text{area\_wt}_j \;=\; \frac{\text{area}\!\left(\text{catchment} \cap \text{tract}_j\right)} {\text{area}\!\left(\text{tract}_j\right)},

the fraction of that tract’s land that sits inside the catchment, running from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (the tract is entirely inside). The shading uses a viridis scale locked to that fixed [0, 1] domain, so a given weight always reads as the same color. This weight is exactly the lever the next stage pulls when it blends tracts; its derivation lives in vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS").

cacs_plot_site_intersection(
  site_id  = ANCHOR,
  iso_sf   = fixture$iso_sf,
  tract_sf = fixture$tract_sf,
  sites_df = fixture$sites_df
)

What to look for. Dark tracts carry a high area weight: most or all of the tract lies inside the catchment, so it pulls hard on every downstream number. The interior tracts near the Vulcan should read dark — close to 1.0, fully enclosed — while the pale tracts trace the catchment boundary: those are slivers, tracts the ten-minute polygon clips only at the edge, contributing just a fraction of their residents. Hover or click any tract to read its GEOID and exact area_wt in the popup. The contrast between the dark core and the pale rim is the visual fingerprint of area weighting, and it is what makes catchment estimates more honest than a crude “is the tract’s centroid inside?” rule: a tract that is 18% inside is counted as 18% inside, not all-or-nothing.

Stage 3 — a weighted ACS variable

Stage 3 answers how is one ACS indicator distributed across the catchment? Here we map B17001_002, the count of people with income below the poverty level. Because it is a count, cacs_intersect_weight() aggregates it as an area-weighted sum: a tract that is half inside the catchment contributes half of its poverty count. Each tract is drawn as a choropleth of its raw ACS estimate, with the ten-minute outline laid on top for reference. Each tract popup reports its GEOID, the variable code, the estimate, the margin of error (MOE — the half-width of the 90% confidence band the Census publishes with every ACS figure), the tract’s area_wt, and area_wt × estimate, which is that tract’s contribution to the site total.

cacs_plot_site_weighted(
  site_id  = ANCHOR,
  iso_sf   = fixture$iso_sf,
  tract_sf = fixture$tract_sf,
  acs_sf   = fixture$acs_sf,
  variable = "B17001_002",
  sites_df = fixture$sites_df
)

What to look for. Read the spread of color across the tracts inside the outline. An even shade would mean poverty is roughly uniform across the catchment; a sharp dark-to-light gradient flags internal heterogeneity that a single catchment average would paper over. Cross-check the deepest-shaded tracts against Stage 2: a tract that is dark in both maps — a high poverty count and a high area weight — is the one driving the catchment poverty total hardest. That area_wt × estimate line in each popup is exactly the quantity Stage 4 sums up.

Mapping a different indicator

Swap the variable argument for any code in your ACS data, and set variable_family to match so the palette and popup units stay correct. For example, variable = "B19013_001" with variable_family = "median_proxy" for median household income, or variable = "B23025_005" (the unemployed count) with the default variable_family = "spatial_total" for a count. The family controls the ColorBrewer palette and how the popup labels the value, so match it to the kind of measure: "spatial_total" for counts, "area_weighted_scalar_proxy" for scalar proxies, "median_proxy" for medians.

Stage 4 — the headline rates

Stage 4 compresses the whole tract-level panel into one site and one popup. Click the site marker to read the five curated rates for this Birmingham catchment — poverty_rate, snap_rate, ssi_rate, unemp_rate, and labor_force_participation — each as an estimate ± 90% MOE band, alongside the count of contributing tracts for the numerator and denominator (n_tracts_num, n_tracts_den). The exact figures live in the popup; read them straight from the marker.

cacs_plot_site_rates(
  site_id    = ANCHOR,
  iso_sf     = fixture$iso_sf,
  run_result = fixture$run_result,
  sites_df   = fixture$sites_df
)

What to look for. Read each rate together with the width of its ± MOE band, which tells you how precisely the estimate is pinned down — a tight band is a confident number, a wide one is a number to quote carefully. Two flags in the popup mark the limits of reliability. First, if a rate’s MOE had to be computed with the conservative fallback formula rather than the requested one, its name is prefixed with an asterisk. Second, if an estimate could not be formed at all — say a carrier variable failed to resolve on one side of the ratio — the cell comes back NA. For this clean Birmingham snapshot all five rates resolve normally, with no asterisks and no NAs, but those markers are the first things to scan for on a real run. The full NA-propagation rule is in the “Failure propagation” section of ?cacs_run.

All four in one call: cacs_plot_site_pipeline()

You rarely build the four maps by hand. cacs_plot_site_pipeline() runs all four stage functions above with one shared set of site and styling arguments and returns a single cacs_site_plot_pipeline object — a classed list of four leaflet widgets. Printing it does not draw anything; its print() method just lists the accessors, so you can render exactly the stage you want, at the console or in a Quarto chunk.

maps <- cacs_plot_site_pipeline(
  site_id    = ANCHOR,
  iso_sf     = fixture$iso_sf,
  tract_sf   = fixture$tract_sf,
  acs_sf     = fixture$acs_sf,
  run_result = fixture$run_result,
  sites_df   = fixture$sites_df,
  variable   = "B17001_002"
)
print(maps)
# Display any single stage by its accessor. We show the rate-summary stage
# here because its one popup pulls together the entire upstream pipeline:
# isochrone + intersection + area weighting + MOE propagation.
maps$rates

All four accessors — maps$isochrone, maps$intersection, maps$weighted, and maps$rates — are ordinary leaflet HTML widgets, so you can save any of them to a standalone HTML report with htmlwidgets::saveWidget() or drop one straight into a Shiny leafletOutput() slot. See ?cacs_plot_site_pipeline for the full argument list.

Interpretation guide: which question each stage answers

The value of splitting the pipeline into four maps is that each one answers a different question — exactly how you want to narrate it in a policy report, because each map maps to a different reviewer concern.

  • Stage 1 (isochrone) — “How far does my site’s catchment reach?” The accessibility question. The shape and reach of the ten-minute polygon show a decision-maker the geographic area the site is responsible for, and whether the setting is dense-urban or sprawling.
  • Stage 2 (intersection / area weight) — “How do my catchment and the Census tracts overlap?” The methodological-transparency question. Showing the weight itself lets a reviewer verify, tract by tract, how much each one feeds the downstream estimate, and see that edge slivers are down-weighted rather than counted whole — no hidden all-or-nothing assignment.
  • Stage 3 (weighted variable) — “How is one indicator distributed inside my catchment?” The spatial-heterogeneity question. The tract choropleth exposes internal disparities that a single catchment average would mask, and points to the neighborhoods driving the total.
  • Stage 4 (rates summary) — “What are my site’s five headline rates, in one line?” The final-reporting question. Estimates ± MOE and contributing tract counts fit in one popup and transfer cleanly to a report table, while the fallback asterisk and any NA make the limits of each estimate visible at the same moment.
